newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast to mull cocoa quality, auction changes.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast to mull cocoa quality, auction changes.

text.p: Ivory Coast will consider cocoa quality and export contract auction revisions after talks with the industry and donors, but a date for decisions has not been set, an Ivorian official told Reuters on Friday.

Ivory Coast has come under criticism from the market for loosening quality checks and for setting up in May 1996 an auction system that the market believes encourages overbidding for export contracts and price speculation.

"The principle problems from reforms are the functioning of the electronic auction system. We are also preoccupied with keeping Ivory Coast's cocoa quality," said Cocoa Consultative Committee president Philippe Mian, who is also technical adviser to Ivorian Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan.
"We will adopt a common position," he told Reuters on the sidelines of committee talks involving the International Cocoa Organization, the industry, plus donor and Ivorian officials.
The talks end on Friday.
Ivory Coast has reduced the role of the Caistab state commodity marketing board since 1994, privatising internal marketing and directing bids for export rights through the auction.
"The talks have been very positive," said World Bank spokesman Jean-Claude Balcet, who is monitoring Ivorian progress with a $150 million ASAC loan for adjusting the agricultural sector.
"The talks have only been consultative but will lay the groundwork for another ASAC mission around mid-April," he added.
Auction rule changes were not imminent, he said.
Exporters' GEPEX trade body president Rene Ekra restated proposals for auction rule changes, of which only two have been accepted by the World Bank.
"We might accept GEPEX proposals if data yet to be supplied by the Caistab shows they are warranted," said Balcet.
Variable price for cocoa according to quality criteria, along with a new marketing price structure for bulk cocoa shipping had also been discussed, World Bank officials said.
Mian said Ivorian cocoa trade statistics were unreliable.

"We need to have reliable statistics on harvesting and and marketing of cocoa," said Mian, echoing comments to Reuters by Ivory Coast's Agriculture Minister in November. "Since withdrawal of the Caistab these can no longer be guaranteed."
Other delegates said quality concerns had not arisen soley due to Caistab reforms but partly due to CFA franc currency devalution in 1994, the weather and the use of hybrids that demanded more care.
Ivorian cocoa stocks reached warehouse capacity of nearly 400,000 tonnes in January as exporters faced low world prices after bidding high to win export clearance in the first place.
CAOBISCO (European confectionary body) delegate Ian Taylor said the problem was real.
"The risk of contract default in a rising market is one of the most serious challenges facing the cocoa market," he said.
Delegates said the Caistab risked losing payments from exporters caught out with too much cocoa and limited export opportunities.
Industry delegates said auction changes were needed soon.
"The GEPEX proposals could be put into place to see if they work. But we need to hurry up, " he added, as forward selling for the 1997/98 season was already under way.
Rule changes under discussion would mean bidders winning contracts at the price they bid rather than at the second highest price.
Contracts would be spread out between five top bidders and a rule setting 15 percent of contracts for foreign traders and 85 percent for local exporters would also be reviewed.
Donors want farmgate prices for cocoa clarified and say debts up the cocoa chain encourage hasty harvesting, drying and selling by farmers.
"It should be made clear once and for all whether the farm price (345 CFA a kilo) price is indicative or fixed."
Mian said other issues included the quality of sacks used to transport cocoa.
